content: The use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as cobicistat, is contraindicated with venetoclax during the initial ramp-up dosing phase. Cobicistat increases venetoclax levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism in the liver and intestines. Similarly, darunavir can elevate venetoclax levels by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. If a P-gp inhibitor must be used, the venetoclax dose should be reduced by at least 50%, and patients should be closely monitored for signs of toxicity. Cobicistat also increases the levels of venlafaxine, verapamil, vilanterol/fluticasone furoate, vilazodone, vinblastine, vincristine, vincristine liposomal, vinorelbine, voclosporin, vorapaxar, voriconazole, vortioxetine, warfarin, zileuton, zaleplon, zanubrutinib, ziprasidone, zolpidem, zonisamide, and zuranolone by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. In many cases, alternative drugs should be considered, or therapy should be modified with close monitoring for adverse effects. For example, when co-administering zanubrutinib with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, the dose should be reduced to 80 mg daily, and therapy should be adjusted as needed for adverse reactions. Patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV who discontinue antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) containing emtricitabine or tenofovir are at risk of severe acute hepatitis B exacerbations. Hepatic function should be closely monitored for several months after discontinuation, and anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted. ARTs are not approved for treating chronic HBV infection, and their safety and efficacy in HIV-1 and HBV co-infected patients have not been established. Darunavir, a protease inhibitor, selectively inhibits the cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors, preventing the formation of mature virus particles. Emtricitabine, a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI), interferes with HIV viral DNA polymerase, inhibiting viral replication. Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), another NRTI, is a targeted prodrug of tenofovir with high antiviral efficacy and an improved renal and bone safety profile compared to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF). Patients receiving ARTs may experience body fat redistribution, including central obesity, peripheral wasting, and a cushingoid appearance. Increased bleeding has been reported in hemophilia patients treated with HIV protease inhibitors. Severe skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, have been reported with darunavir. Immune reconstitution syndrome, autoimmune disorders, and postmarketing cases of renal impairment, including acute renal failure and Fanconi syndrome, have also been observed. Darunavir contains a sulfonamide moiety, so patients with sulfonamide allergies should be monitored closely. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with nucleoside analogs like emtricitabine. New-onset diabetes mellitus, hyperglycemia, and exacerbation of preexisting diabetes have been reported during postmarketing surveillance of HIV protease inhibitors. ARTs should be taken with food, and tablets can be split if necessary, but the entire dose must be consumed immediately. Medications should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F) in tightly closed containers with desiccants to protect from moisture.
